items.title: Suspense
items.author: Henry Seton Merriman
items.content:
Theo Trist and Brenda Gilholme have known one another since childhood. Trist has become a renowned war correspondent for influential newspapers in London and Paris, dispatched to dangerous areas of the globe to report on the most terrible events imaginable. Brenda, until now in the shadow of her sister, a celebrated society beauty, has lived the life of the mind, immersing herself in studies of languages, mathematics, theology, and political economy—a life which Victorian society doesn’t value for its daughters, but which Trist admires in the observant and analytical Brenda. Mrs. Wylie, a mutual friend who has supported each of them throughout their formative years, knows that their respective intelligence, and their senses of honor, duty, and self-sacrifice, set them apart from their peers and drive them to make the most of themselves. Those same strengths also divide and distance them from one another—and, as Mrs. Wylie knows, time is on no one’s side.

is one of Henry Seton Merriman’s more philosophical novels. In meta-commentary, the author makes plain his acceptance of Victorian views on social roles, expectations, and responsibilities, while also celebrating those who are courageous enough to stand apart from that society to live their own lives. Though an earlier of Merriman’s works, it still displays the intricate plotting, character development, and attention to place and history which are characteristic of his later works. Though its narrative and dialogue fit squarely within the framework of contemporary Victorian fiction, nevertheless demonstrates the best of that structure, even as Merriman shows with his subsequent works his desire and capability to rise above it.

items.title: The Emperor of Portugallia
items.author: Selma Lagerlöf
items.content:
Jan Andersson is a poor crofter. The only thing that brings him joy is his daughter Glory, but when the family finds itself in need of money, she moves to Stockholm to look for a job. At first Jan is despondent, especially as Glory very quickly stops sending letters. But as time goes on, Jan begins to piece together what happened to Glory in Stockholm—though his conclusions differ wildly from everyone else’s.

Blending family drama with social critique, Selma Lagerlöf explores the ways in which community and generational relations can be affected by forces both beyond and within our control, and how redemption is possible, if we so choose.

Lagerlöf considered titling the novel , alluding to the generational conflicts central to both the novel and the play. Today The Emperor of Portugallia is considered a classic of Swedish literature, with multiple adaptations, including the now lost 1925 Hollywood film and a 1992 series for Swedish public television.

items.title: The Mystery of the Barranca
items.author: Herman Whitaker
items.content:
William Thornton and Robert Seyd are two American friends who share an interest in mining. They make an agreement that whoever finds a good prospect has to contact the other so that they can work together to exploit the mine. The day to honor this pact finally comes when Robert finds a rich copper mine in Guerrero, Mexico.

On the way to the mine, William is struck by the beauty of an elegant young woman, accompanied by a large Siberian wolfhound, at a local train station. As the train approaches, the dog leaps onto the tracks. Robert, acting quickly, gets the dog to safety in the nick of time. The girl’s companion—the nephew of the general who owns the land under the mine—offers the American duo men and mules to transport their equipment to their destination.

What appears to be a stroke of good luck ends up becoming a prelude to a seemingly endless wave of challenges, as the bad omens surrounding the mine, and the general's animosity towards Americans, threaten to lead William and Robert down a path of treachery and darkness.

items.title: Moral Letters to Lucilius
items.author: Seneca
items.content:
Seneca was a Stoic philosopher and statesman in Rome’s early post-Augustan era. He was Nero’s tutor, and then his advisor when Nero became emperor in 54 CE. After Seneca retired from public life, he wrote a series of letters to his friend Lucilius, the procurator of Sicily. These letters were circulated right before Seneca’s death in 65 CE, when Nero forced him to commit suicide for his alleged involvement in a conspiracy.

These letters, which were written for widespread publication as well as directly to Lucilius, mainly focus on guiding the reader to a life well-lived. At times, the advice is regarding specific personal issues, such as when he gives a review of a book written by Lucilius. Other letters give Seneca’s thoughts on broader issues like slavery, independence of thought, and virtue. Through all of them, his Stoicism shines through, whether in his metaphysics (like when he writes on “the god within us”) or in his focus on how virtue is the only good. His diverse interests are also on display, as when he addresses current events (like the burning of Lyons), or when he speculates on science (like when he offers his thoughts on animal instincts).

These letters have been popular and influential since their initial circulation, and were widely read from the Roman period, up through the Middle Ages, and into the Renaissance, where Michel de Montaigne used them as a model for his . They remain highly regarded today for their practical and sage advice.

items.title: Robur the Conqueror
items.author: Jules Verne
items.content: , also published as The Clipper of the Clouds, opens in Philadelphia at a meeting of the Weldon Institute, a club of balloon enthusiasts. A stranger named Robur asks to address the members, then tells them that the future belongs to heavier-than-air machines. He mocks the club’s giant balloon, the , and insults its members until the meeting erupts in chaos. That night he kidnaps Uncle Prudent, the club’s president, Phil Evans, its secretary, and Frycollin, Prudent’s servant. He takes them captive aboard the , the flying machine he built, and flies them around the world to prove his point. After the captives escape, the story returns to Philadelphia for the first launch of the , where the appears in the sky to challenge it.

items.title: Of One Blood
items.author: Pauline E. Hopkins
items.content:
Attending medical school in Boston, Reuel Briggs has neither wealth nor the good looks of the upper-class white society with which he surrounds himself. He is, however, incredibly talented, and has a rare gift in the psychological study of mysticism and supernatural phenomenon. Even if his peers aren’t too keen on him, they can’t help but be awed by his talent, and subsequently call on his aid in reaching out to the minds of the sick and dying who would otherwise be lost. Though this field of mysticism is his life’s work and sole talent, it may soon be his downfall as it leads him down a dark path of secrets and discoveries.

was first published serially in The Colored American Magazine, which Hopkins edited at the time. Written at the turn of the century and shortly after the Civil War, Hopkins explores the legacy of slavery, questions of identity, and the bounds of love and loyalty.

items.title: The Sowers
items.author: Henry Seton Merriman
items.content:
With , a story ranging from the upper class drawing-rooms of London, Paris, and St. Petersburg to the vast estates and peasant villages of the Russian steppe, Henry Seton Merriman enjoyed his greatest popular success. Its protagonist is a young man of strong ideals and character who is known to his friends and London society as Paul Howard Alexis, to the vicious Russian aristocracy and the thousands of resentful peasants on his estate as Prince Pavlo Alexis, and to those same impoverished thousands as the “Moscow Doctor” sent by God, whose tireless, compassionate, selfless care sustains them. This enigmatic man is understood only by his closest advisor, friend, and confidant, Karl Steinmetz, a cosmopolitan utopian philosopher given to bouts of cynicism and sentimentalism. Together they resolve, come what may, to carry out the work of a charitable organization banned by the Russian state but crucial to the well-being of millions of oppressed peasants.

The dangers are tremendous. The leadership of their organization is exiled by the Tsar’s secret police; nobles concerned with their peasants’ welfare are undermined by their peers; those same peasants, suspicious and superstitious, fear that anyone could be a spy or that any change in their lives will only deepen their misery; revolutionaries seek to exploit the growing unrest for their own political ends, while others seek to exploit it for their personal advantage. As Alexis and Steinmetz navigate this web of treachery, they realize that the greatest dangers and betrayals may come from those closest to them.

In , Merriman wrote with authority about the physical and political landscape of Russia, and with passion concerning those liberal ideals which became more evident in his later novels. For contemporary readers, the novel presented an exotic, mysterious place, the Russian Empire of the Romanovs, to which few traveled and which even fewer understood. As other European empires slowly changed and liberalized, Russia, with its vast spaces and rural millions, seemed increasingly anachronistic. Several of the more idealistic characters in the novel give voice to the author’s own sense that Russia would soon face an existential crisis when its peasantry finally rose up against those who had oppressed them for centuries, though the nature of such a revolution was unclear, and its trigger might not come in their lifetimes. For today’s reader, with the benefit of historical hindsight, those suggestions are uncannily prescient.

Published in 1896, anticipated the first Russian revolution by nine years. The extreme violence which attended the final fall of the Romanovs and their empire in 1917 occurred just fourteen years after Merriman’s own premature death in 1903.

items.title: Beautiful Stories from Shakespeare
items.author: E. Nesbit
items.content:
Two young couples, lost in an enchanted wood, are manipulated by quarreling fairies. A magician and his daughter entertain visitors he shipwrecked on their enchanted island. A king divides his lands unequally among his three daughters according to how well they flatter him. A witches’ prophecy sets a Scottish general on a tragic path.

Beautiful Stories from Shakespeare is a collection of retellings of twenty of William Shakespeare’s plays by noted children’s author E. Nesbit. Each play is condensed to its core story and told using simple language that children can understand. While some quotations from Shakespeare are retained, the emphasis is on the stories rather than the language. The collection contains thirteen comedies and seven tragedies, but none of the histories.

By 1907 Nesbit was well known for children’s novels such as and . This collection expands on 1897’s The Children’s Shakespeare, which retells twelve of these plays. It follows in the tradition of prose retellings for children established by Charles and Mary Lamb’s 1807 .

items.title: The Storm of Steel
items.author: Ernst Jünger
items.content:
Ernst Jünger was a German officer commanding storm troopers during World War I. This, his memoir of his time on the front, is one of the very first literary accounts of the Great War.

Jünger begins his story as a private entering training in the Champagne region. He continues on to take part in various battles, climbing the ranks until attaining command of a regiment and accumulating fourteen different hits from bullets or shrapnel. His career ends near the very end of the war: his lung is punctured by a bullet while his men die all around him, and he’s sent to the rear to convalesce in the war’s waning months.

The realities of this new style of war are described in a matter-of-fact and mostly apolitical way. Despite the obscene horrors Jünger graphically recounts, he seems stoic, even apathetic, about his role in the war, and about the destruction it caused. As he narrates battle after battle in gruesome detail, he falls back on a sense of “war without anger,” framing himself as a cog in an emotionless machine and his enemies as deserving of respect for their valor, and not hatred for their actions. Even as his superiors issue orders that he can clearly see will lead his men into the bloody meat grinder, Jünger remains obedient, patriotic, and driven by a sense of duty and national pride.

The first edition was published in 1920, shortly after the war’s end. Jünger revised the book several times, transforming its raw diary style into a more literary one in 1924. Consequently, the book sold incredibly well, allowing Jünger to lead a post-war career as a writer. Its emphasis on nationalism made it a favorite of Nazi propagandists in the early 1930s, in contrast with Erich Maria Remarque’s equally matter-of-fact but more clearly anti-war All Quiet on the Western Front, which the Nazis banned. Jünger, who was not a Nazi, again revised it in 1934 in an attempt to make it less attractive as nationalistic propaganda, but despite his attempts the book remained a popular one both with the Wehrmacht and with the public.

items.title: On the Making of Man
items.author: Gregory of Nyssa
items.content: is an early treatise on theological anthropology, the area of Christian theology that inquires into human nature with respect to God. In the treatise, the 4th century bishop and theologian Gregory of Nyssa interprets the creation narrative found in the first three chapters of the Book of Genesis. In particular, he expounds on the verse Genesis 1:27, the textual basis of the Christian doctrine of (i.e. that humanity is made in God’s image). He argues that, being made in the likeness of divine sovereignty, human beings possess inherent dignity. This resemblance to God lies in humanity’s capability to possess godlike virtues, such as purity and freedom from passion. In order to refute opposing Christian and non-Christian views on human nature, Gregory ponders the soul’s relationship with the body, arguing that neither the body nor the soul preceded the other, but that both were co-created. He also argues for the possibility of the universal restoration of creation to perfection (a controversial doctrine known as ) on the basis of the finitude of evil.
